newsitem.title: JAPAN: KEY JGB YIELD SEEN SLIDING TO TWO PCT--ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: KEY JGB YIELD SEEN SLIDING TO TWO PCT--ANALYSTS.

text.p: The yield of the key long-term Japanese government bond is likely to fall to two percent or less over the next month or two due to a soft economy and worries about the troubled construction sector, analysts and bond traders said on Friday.

"Deflation continues to be a reality and the hope that weak data was just the result of April's sales tax increase is now fading, and people are coming to terms with the broader economic decline," said William Campbell, yen fixed income strategist at JP Morgan Securities Asia in Tokyo.
Campbell said he expected the benchmark 182nd 10-year JGB yield to fall below two percent by the end of September.

Concern about the financial health of construction firms, reflected in a recent sharp rise in yields on their bonds, has been another driving force behind the recent JGB price rally, traders and analysts said.

"General contractors are suffering from bad loan problems and they have also been hit hard by the government's fiscal tightening policies. The brakes have been applied too strongly to fiscal spending," said Masuhisa Kobayashi, vice president with the yen-bond trading desk at Merrill Lynch Inc Asia.
Kobayashi said he felt the key JGB yield may fall to 1.95 percent over the next month.
The problems of Japan's construction firms have come back into the spotlight since two mid-sized general contractors failed in July.

"Employees at Japan's construction firms account for about 10 percent of the nation's workforce, so financial problems at such firms can have a very large impact on the overall economy," Merrill Lynch's Kobayashi said.

Four-year bonds issued by Fujita Corp, maturing in September 2001 with a coupon rate of 3.0 percent, and five-year bonds issued by JDC Corp, maturing in July 2002 with a coupon rate of 2.95 percent, were offered at rates of nearly 10 percent on Friday, or more than 800 basis points above the corresponding rates for interest rate swaps, traders said.
The continuing decline in commercial land prices is another positive factor for JGBs, analysts said.

Banks will be caught in a double bind if interest rates rise while the value of their commercial land holdings is falling, so the Bank of Japan (BOJ) is likely to avoid raising rates for some time, said Takeshi Naito, assistant general manager for market intelligence at Daiwa Securities Co's bond department.
"Banks that need to liquidate problem loans will have to sell land they accepted as collateral from borrowers, so there is room for a further fall in commercial land prices," Naito said.
JP Morgan's Campbell said it could be argued that current JGB yields are still high, if the fall in commercial land prices were used as a yard stick for inflation.

"Yesterday's data showed commercial real estate in Tokyo fell 2.5 percent in April-June from the previous quarter. Depending on how you annualise that, you end up with price falls in the order of 10 percent per year on commercial real estate. Now if that is your measure of inflation, the real JGB yields are quite high," he said.
The next key event for JGBs will be July industrial output data due at the end of the month, but analysts said the data is unlikely to reverse the current firmness in JGB prices.
"Forecasts of manufacturers' production in August and September will also be released, but I think...the forecasts will be relatively weak," Daiwa's Naito said.

The key JGB yield may fall as low as two percent before the release of the BOJ's next "tankan" survey of corporate sentiment, perhaps as early as late September, said Yasuo Yoshida, senior bond trader at Paribas Capital Markets Ltd in Tokyo.
"While July industrial output data may cause some waves in the market, there is little chance the market will begin factoring in a rise in interest rates before the next tankan survey," Yoshida said.
